claims.text: Coupling machine-learning interatomic potentials with enhanced sampling can accurately reproduce solid- and liquid-phase free energies at fusion conditions.
The proposed workflow can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The proposed workflow will substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
The cost advantage will be particularly significant for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The intended systems include elemental metals, binary alloys, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys near melting.
The machine-learning potentials will be trained on rigorous ab initio free-energy data.
Interatomic potentials can act as computational surrogates for atomistic calculations in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Such surrogate potentials can provide high-fidelity results for high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced sampling will provide complete exploration of the solid and liquid configurational landscapes.
Replica-exchange metadynamics can adequately sample anharmonic vibrational modes relevant to fusion free energies.
Enhanced sampling with an interatomic potential can retain electron–vibration coupling.
The resulting phase free energies and fusion observables will have fidelity similar to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The workflow will reduce computational time by approximately one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The workflow will provide better throughput than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
The proposed applicability range is approximately 1000–1600 K near melting.
Sparse training data at extreme compositions may cause machine-learning interpolation errors.
Complete enhanced sampling may be difficult in highly complex configurational spaces.
The method is to be benchmarked against explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD using solid and liquid free energies, fusion temperature, entropy contributions, and computational cost.
Failure to obtain roughly a tenfold speedup while keeping free-energy differences and derived observables within ±5% of explicit ab initio results will falsify the hypothesis.
